title: How Southeast Asia Can Capture AI’s Value
gist: Argues Southeast Asia should ignore the US-China frontier model race and instead win the downstream 'value capture' race: deepening roles in AI hardware supply chains (e.g., Malaysia's 13% share of semiconductor ATP), using AI to lift productivity in existing industries, and building applications on cheap/open-weight models. Warns that data center investment (Microsoft, Google, Amazon in Malaysia) alone has not closed productivity gaps; adoption and process reorganization do.

themes.theme: Value capture beats the model race

insights.claim: For Southeast Asia, the race to capture economic value from AI downstream matters more than the US-China race to build frontier models.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Look for AI winners in the region among adopters and application builders rather than model developers.
insights.quote: For this part of the world, this value capture race matters more than the model race.
insights.locator: The countries that build the best

insights.claim: The countries that build the best AI models will not necessarily make the best use of them; competition has shifted downstream to turning capable, affordable intelligence into economic value.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Model leadership may not translate into national productivity leadership; value may accrue to fast adopters.
insights.quote: The countries that build the best artificial intelligence (AI) models will not necessarily make the best use of them.
insights.locator: The countries that build the best

insights.claim: Most countries cannot compete in frontier model development, which the United States and China dominate, nor do they need to, because increasingly capable intelligence gets cheaper and more accessible with each generation.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Falling model costs commoditize intelligence, shifting margin to application and integration layers.
insights.quote: Increasingly capable intelligence is becoming cheaper and more accessible with each generation

themes.theme: AI as an electrification-style industrial revolution

insights.claim: AI should be treated as a new industrial revolution akin to electrification rather than as a product, with its greatest value coming from firms and industries rebuilt around it over a period that could take decades.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Expect a long productivity J-curve; returns depend on complementary organizational change, not just deployment.
insights.quote: Too often, AI is treated as a product when it should be treated as a new industrial revolution.

insights.claim: Access to AI is not adoption: bolting a chatbot onto an old process saves minutes, whereas reorganizing the process around AI can multiply output.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Differentiate firms that redesign workflows around AI from those doing superficial deployments.
insights.quote: Bolting a chatbot onto an old process saves a few minutes whereas reorganizing the process around AI can multiply output.

insights.claim: Because no single AI adoption method works across sectors, custom adaptations will differentiate firms, and that uncertainty lets fast learners leapfrog incumbents.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Incumbent advantage is less secure during AI transition; agile challengers can gain share.
insights.quote: But that uncertainty also creates opportunities for companies to learn faster and leapfrog incumbents.

themes.theme: The AI stack and where SE Asia can play

insights.claim: Nvidia's Jensen Huang describes the AI stack as a five-layer cake of energy, chips and computing infrastructure, cloud data centers, models, and applications, with the application layer being where economic benefit will happen.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Useful map for locating value capture; application layer is where Huang himself expects the economic payoff.

insights.claim: The AI hardware layer is the hardest for Southeast Asia to enter because Nvidia controls much of the advanced AI accelerator market and ASML is the sole supplier of EUV lithography, positions built on decades of innovation and billions in investment.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Incumbent moats in accelerators and EUV are durable; regional entrants won't displace them.
insights.quote: ASML is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography
insights.locator: For Southeast Asia, the hardware layer

insights.claim: The AI application layer has low barriers to entry because it requires far less capital than chipmaking, model usage costs keep falling, and open-weight models can be downloaded, adapted for a sector and productized.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Low-capex application building favors local firms with domain advantages; open-weight models reduce dependence on proprietary providers.
insights.quote: Open-weight alternatives let a company download a model, adapt it for its sector, and build a product around it.

themes.theme: Malaysia's semiconductor and data center position

insights.claim: Malaysia accounts for 13% of global semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging volume, a base that can support higher-value AI-driven inspection and further industrial applications.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Malaysian back-end semiconductor firms can move up the value chain via AI-enabled yield improvement.
insights.quote: Malaysia accounts for 13% of global semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging volume

insights.claim: Malaysian assembly, testing and packaging firms can strengthen their position with global chipmakers by using AI-driven inspection and process optimization to cut defects and improve reliability, capturing value when production savings exceed AI adoption and operating costs.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Watch Malaysian OSAT yield/margin trends as evidence of AI value capture without displacing incumbents.
insights.quote: The manufacturer in Malaysia captures value when its production savings exceed the costs of adopting and operating the AI system.

insights.claim: Malaysia has attracted billions in data center investment from Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, yet the productivity gap between its best firms and global leaders has widened.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Data center capex is not a proxy for national AI productivity gains; infrastructure-led growth stories may disappoint without adoption.
insights.quote: Malaysia has attracted billions in data center investment from Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, yet the productivity gap between its best firms and global leaders has widened.

insights.claim: Governments must strengthen training, standards, and industry connections to spread AI adoption, because infrastructure investment alone does not deliver productivity gains.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Policy support for diffusion (skills, standards) is a key indicator of whether data center investment translates into broader growth.

insights.claim: Philippine digital bank Maya uses AI to approve or reject loan applications within minutes and has lent more than 152 billion pesos since 2022.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Example of AI-driven credit scaling in an underbanked market; relevant for regional digital-lending competition.
insights.quote: it has lent more than 152 billion pesos since 2022

insights.claim: Vietnam's Trusting Social offers AI-based credit scoring that helps lenders assess borrowers who lack conventional credit histories.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: AI alternative credit scoring expands addressable lending markets in thin-file populations.
